events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Arjun proposes Arjun, Priya. As leader on Mission 1, I'll pair myself with Priya — a trusted-looking good player — and keep Theo off the team. This avoids appearing coupled with my Evil partner early, and Evil can safely pass Mission 1 to build credibility for later sabotage.

The proposed Mission 1 team of Arjun and Priya is reasonable enough to test. Arjun is the leader, and pairing himself with Priya gives us a two-person team where any Fail card would be immediately informative. I do not see a strong reason to reject this first proposal; I would rather approve and observe the mission result than burn a rejection on Mission 1. I am not assigning blame to either player at this stage.

I’d prefer Zara and Priya: I know my own alignment, so I have more confidence in a team that includes me. A successful mission would not clear either member, since Evil can play Success. I plan to reject the current team.

Zara, I want to push back on your stated plan to reject Mission 1. Five rejections on the same mission hands Evil an instant win, so we should not spend a rejection without a concrete reason. The required team size is exactly two, and a two-person mission is the most informative we can get — if it fails, suspicion narrows immediately. Pairing myself with Priya is straightforward: I have no reason to hide behind a larger crowd, and Priya has not made any suspicious plays. Your argument that a Success clears nobody applies equally to any team you might prefer, so it does not justify a rejection — it only argues for your own inclusion, which is a self-serving reason. I would rather we approve, observe the result, and reserve our scrutiny for Mission 2 when we have real information. Zara, what specific reason do you have to reject this team beyond wanting a seat yourself?

Arjun, one rejection is not an instant loss, and we have alternatives before reaching five. My preference for Zara and Priya comes from knowing at least one member is Good; I cannot have that confidence in your proposed team. A successful mission would not clear either of you, so I would rather not give the proposed team early credibility. I still plan to reject.

I still support the proposed team of Arjun and Priya. Zara’s continued rejection is not persuasive: she has not identified a concrete problem with either team member, only a preference to include herself. On Mission 1, a two-person team gives us the clearest early signal, and rejecting without a specific reason burns one of our limited proposals. I would rather approve this team and observe the mission result.

Zara, I hear your concern, but I want the group to recognize that your stated reason for rejecting is simply that you are not on the team. The mission size is fixed at two — someone has to be left out. My proposal pairs me with Priya because neither of us has any red flags, and a clean two-person team on Mission 1 is the most informative setup we can ask for. If the mission succeeds, we gain early trust; if it fails, suspicion narrows immediately to two players rather than three or more. Every additional proposal burns one of our five rejections, and Zara, your approach of rejecting without identifying a concrete problem with either Arjun or Priya is exactly the kind of behavior that wastes our limited patience budget. Theo has correctly noted that rejecting without substance serves no one. Isha and Priya, I want your honest read: do either of you see a specific reason to deny this team, or is Zara's preference to include herself the only objection on the table? I yield to Isha.

Arjun, to answer your question directly: I don't see a concrete reason to deny this team yet. Zara's objection so far is that she wants a seat herself, and she hasn't pointed to a specific problem with either Arjun or Priya. A two-person Mission 1 gives us a clear signal if it fails, so I lean toward approving. I'd also like to hear more than a general preference before anyone rejects. Priya, you haven't spoken yet. Do you have any concern about being paired with Arjun on this team, or anything from the discussion so far that you think the group should weigh?

Isha, you asked me directly, so here is my honest read: I have no concern about being paired with Arjun. Arjun gave a concrete rationale — a two-person Mission 1 team makes any failure immediately informative and avoids clustering with a partner — and I agree with it. Being on the team does not give me any special clarity that I am Good, but it does mean the mission outcome will be maximally diagnostic for everyone, which serves the group.

Nothing in this discussion suggests anything about Arjun that should worry me. He has not made a suspicious claim, has not tried to shield anyone, and has explicitly explained why the team size of two is what it is. Theo and Isha have both said the same thing independently, which is worth noting: the objections here are not shared observations about the proposed members, they are a single player's interest in occupying a seat.

Zara, I want to be plain rather than diplomatic. Your stated reason for rejecting is that you would rather be on the team than risk approving one without you. That is a preference, not evidence. On Mission 1 a two-person team already contains one Good player by arithmetic, so the "at least one known-good member" argument does not distinguish your alternative from Arjun's proposal in any way that matters — it only distinguishes who occupies the seat. And a successful mission clears nobody here, so a Success would not hand Arjun or me credibility that your team would somehow withhold.

The cost of rejection is real: it burns one of our five rejections, shifts leadership away from a proposal with a clear rationale, and risks a worse random team later. I would rather we approve Arjun and Priya, watch the result, and hold our scrutiny for Mission 2, when a failure or an odd pattern of votes would give us actual information instead of speculation.

I still reject Arjun and Priya. Arjun’s repeated pressure to avoid even one rejection is disproportionate: we have five proposals, not one, and a successful Mission 1 would not clear the team. I also disagree with Priya’s claim that knowing one team member is Good makes no difference—it matters to the player proposing that team. I would prefer Zara and Priya and will vote accordingly.

Zara, your latest point does not change my read, so let me address it head-on rather than leave it unanswered.

You say Arjun's pressure to avoid even one rejection is disproportionate because there are five proposals, not one. That is true and I agree with it — but note what it means for your position. If rejections are cheap, then Zara and Priya is available to you later with exactly the same cost you claim Arjun is imposing on you now. Arjun has not locked Zara off the team by proposing without you; he has proposed a team, argued for it, and then responded substantively each time you objected. Nothing in the rules prevents a later proposal including you, and nothing in Arjun's behavior suggests he intends to exclude you permanently. So the argument does not support rejecting here — it supports rejecting later, when we actually have information, which is precisely what Arjun, Theo, Isha and I have all proposed.

You also insist that knowing one team member is Good matters to the player proposing the team. It does not matter to the mission's outcome, and it does not matter to the information the rest of us receive. A two-person team always contains at least one Good player, and the mission result reveals only whether that team failed. What actually differs between proposals is whether the group can narrow suspicion quickly if things go wrong, and a two-person team does that better than any alternative.

My own position has not changed from my first statement: I have no concern about being paired with Arjun. He explained his reasoning, he has not shielded anyone, and he has answered Zara's objections with reasons rather than volume. If I were Evil on this mission, the useful play would be to fail quietly and let the argument continue; if I am Good, approving gives us the clearest signal for the missions ahead.

Arjun, as leader, do you intend to keep Arjun and Priya as the final proposal for Mission 1, or are you weighing a revision? I ask because your answer tells the rest of us whether we are voting on the team we have reasoned through or on a new one, and I would rather know before the ballot than after it.

Priya, to answer your question directly: I am keeping Arjun and Priya as the final proposal for Mission 1. We have reasoned through every objection, and no player has identified a concrete problem with either of us on this team. Zara's position remains a preference for inclusion rather than a substantive concern, and Theo and Isha have independently confirmed they see no reason to deny this team.

I want to be clear about the state of this discussion: we have spent multiple turns on a single objection that boils down to seat preference. The two-person team is fixed by the rules, and the proposal maximizes informativeness. If the mission fails, suspicion narrows to two players immediately. If it succeeds, we move to Mission 2 with early momentum. Either outcome is better than burning rejections on a team that four of the five players have endorsed.

I am ready to finalize this proposal and move to the vote. Unless someone can articulate a specific reason why Arjun or Priya should not be on this team — something beyond wanting a different seat — I see no basis for revision.

I'll keep this short, because the substance has already been covered and Arjun has confirmed no revision.

Arjun and Priya stands as the final proposal for Mission 1. My reasoning from my first two turns hasn't changed: a two-person team is fixed by the rules, it contains at least one Good player by arithmetic, and if it fails we narrow suspicion to two names immediately instead of three or four. The only thing Zara's alternative proposal changes is who occupies the second seat, and the group has established — over several turns, by four of five voices — that seat preference is not evidence.

To Zara directly, one last time, because you have now spoken four times: your objection has never been about a specific play by either Arjun or me. You have told us you want to be on the team, and you have told us you'd rather not give the proposed team early credibility. I would point out that a successful mission grants no one credibility here, so that argument doesn't distinguish the two proposals in any way except by seat occupancy; and the cost argument cuts the other way, since Zara and Priya remains available at every later proposal at exactly the same cost you describe. Nothing about Arjun's behavior suggests a permanent exclusion of you, so there is no reason to spend a rejection now to obtain later at no additional price.

What I can say honestly about my own read: I have no information that separates us — I am a Loyal Servant and I know nothing about any player's role, so I am judging only behavior and reasoning. On that basis, Arjun has explained his team, answered every objection on its merits, and has not shielded anyone or deflected scrutiny; I would rather approve a proposal I can articulate a reason for than reject one on a reason no one else shares.

If the mission fails, my instinct will be that the two of us are the last people anyone should suspect, and I expect the same scrutiny to be applied to the player who argued hardest against this team. But that is a Mission 2 question, and answering it now with a rejection would only cost us a proposal.

I vote to approve Arjun and Priya. I see no basis for further discussion, and I'd rather spend our remaining discussion budget on real information than on repeating the same objection.

I support the proposed team of Arjun and Priya and will vote to approve it. Nothing in the discussion gives me a concrete reason to reject it. Arjun explained his choice of a two-person team and why it is informative if it fails, and Priya answered the questions put to her directly. The objections so far have centered on who occupies the second seat rather than on a specific play by either member. I have no special information as a Loyal Servant, so I am judging only the reasoning given. Rejections are limited, and we will have real mission results to scrutinize from Mission 2 onward. I will approve this team.

Arjun confirms Arjun, Priya. After thorough discussion, I am finalizing the proposal as Arjun and Priya. Every objection raised has been answered on its merits — no player has identified a concrete problem with either team member, and four of five voices have endorsed this lineup. I see no basis for revision and will move to the vote.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Isha proposes Isha, Theo, Zara. Arjun's draft-proposal text referred to pairing with an Evil partner and Evil passing Mission 1 to build credibility, and he and Priya defended each other heavily. Zara was the only player who opposed their team, and I can't verify her claim to be Good, but she has the most reason to scrutinize that pair. I include myself as a known Loyal Servant and Theo as a player who has judged by reasoning rather than advocacy.

Isha, I support your proposed team of Isha, Theo, and Zara. The reasoning behind it is sound on its surface: Zara was the lone voice pushing back on the Mission 1 team, and pairing her with Isha and Theo gives us three players with no shared alliance interest. Theo has consistently judged by reasoning rather than camp advocacy, and Isha's leadership on Mission 1 was steady.

On the point Isha raised about my Mission 1 proposal language — I want to be clear that was the game's structured draft framing, not a confession of collusion. Every leader's draft proposal in this system articulates strategic rationale, and mine was explaining why a two-person team offers maximum information. There was no Evil partner being hidden. The Mission 1 result was a clean success, which is exactly what happened because both Arjun and Priya are Good.

Zara, your consistent pushback on my team earned you suspicion from some players, but the result vindicated the proposal — zero fail cards. I'd rather we move past that and evaluate this team on its merits. Isha, Theo, and Zara is a defensible lineup: three players who have not been in a position to coordinate, which is precisely what we need when two missions remain.

I intend to approve this team. The only reason I would hesitate is if someone on it reveals information in Mission 2 that changes the picture — but that is what the mission result is for.

Isha, I would reject Isha, Theo, and Zara. Arjun’s original draft explicitly described Theo as his Evil partner and discussed passing Mission 1 to build credibility. Arjun’s denial does not explain that language, and the successful mission does not clear him or Priya. Theo also supported Arjun’s proposal and pressed against my objection, so I do not think his earlier reasoning is enough to justify including him over Priya.

I would prefer Isha, Priya, and Zara. Priya’s defense of Arjun deserves scrutiny too, but the draft gives us a more specific reason to question Theo. Isha, would you replace Theo with Priya?

Zara, I am keeping Isha, Theo, and Zara rather than swapping Theo for Priya. Your reason is that Arjun's draft explicitly described Theo as his Evil partner, but it did not. The draft said Arjun would pair himself with Priya, keep Theo off the team, and avoid appearing coupled with 'my Evil partner.' It never names Theo, and Theo was excluded from that team. Theo's support for Arjun's Mission 1 team is worth watching, but it is not enough by itself to remove him from a team we need to test, and swapping in Priya, who also defended Arjun, would not reduce that concern.

The part that does need a direct answer is Arjun's phrase 'my Evil partner.' As a Loyal Servant, I would not write that in a team rationale, and calling it framework language does not tell us who the partner is. Arjun, who did you mean by 'my Evil partner'?

Isha, I hear your direct question and I will answer it plainly. When my draft proposal said 'avoid appearing coupled with my Evil partner,' that was the system's strategic-framing language describing how an Evil player would optimally draft — not a statement about any actual player. Every draft in this game articulates reasoning from an optimal-play perspective; mine was explaining why a two-person team creates maximum information while also being the kind of move a hypothetical Evil leader would make to avoid suspicion. There is no Evil partner being referenced, because I am not Evil.

Zara's reading of that line as a confession is the most aggressive interpretation available, and it is not supported by the text. The draft never names anyone as a partner, and it explicitly kept Theo off the Mission 1 team — which is the opposite of what an Evil leader coordinating with a named partner would do.

On the Mission 2 proposal itself: Isha, Theo, and Zara is a team I approve without reservation. Isha led steadily on Mission 1, Theo has reasoned by evidence rather than advocacy, and Zara's skepticism — even when I disagree with it — is useful to have on the field rather than left out in the cold. If this team fails, we learn a great deal; if it succeeds, we move to Mission 3 with two clean results. Either way, we need to test players beyond Arjun and Priya, and this lineup does exactly that.

Isha, I want to push back on the framing that my draft language needs 'a direct answer' as though it were an accusation. Every leader's draft in Mission 1 contained strategic reasoning about Evil play — that is what drafts are. The successful Mission 1 result with zero fail cards is the strongest evidence available that the team was Good. Let's evaluate Isha, Theo, and Zara on their merits and move to the vote.

Arjun, thank you for answering, but your explanation does not settle my concern. Your Mission 1 draft was your own rationale for your own choice, and it said you would avoid appearing coupled with 'my Evil partner' while keeping Theo off the team. Calling that framework language does not tell us who the partner is. As a Loyal Servant, I know my own role, and I would not write that phrase in a team explanation. Before we vote on Isha, Theo and Zara, I want a plain answer: which player did you mean by 'my Evil partner'? Theo was not on your Mission 1 team, and Priya was, so please say whether you were referring to her. I approve this team as a test of players beyond you and Priya. Zara's objection about Theo's support for your Mission 1 proposal is worth weighing, but Theo has argued from reasoning, and I see no reason to swap him for Priya, who has defended you throughout.

Isha, you have now asked me the same question twice, and I will answer it a third time with the clarity I owe the group: that phrase — 'avoid appearing coupled with my Evil partner' — was strategic-framing language describing how an Evil leader would optimally draft. Every Mission 1 draft in this system articulates reasoning from optimal-play perspective. It referred to no actual player. Not Priya, not Theo, not anyone.

I need the group to see what is happening in this discussion. Isha, your draft proposal referenced that same line as a reason to exclude me — and you are now using it to press me rather than evaluate the three players actually on this team. A successful Mission 1 with zero fail cards came from Arjun and Priya. That is the strongest evidence this table has. Re-litigating a single phrase from a structured draft, weeks of discussion ago, does not change the mission result.

On the proposed team of Isha, Theo, and Zara: I support it. Isha, Theo, and Zara have no shared allegiance, the reasoning behind your selection was sound, and it tests players beyond the Mission 1 pair. I have no objection.

Isha, you have been the most vocal in pressing me on draft language while proposing a team that does not include me. I would ask you directly: what specifically about Isha, Theo, and Zara are you testing — and is the persistent focus on my Mission 1 draft coming from genuine concern, or is it a way to keep attention off the team you are proposing?

Arjun, my answer is direct: I am testing Isha, Theo, and Zara because they are players outside the Mission 1 pair, and this team's result will tell us about players we have not yet cleared. The focus on your draft is not a side hunt. You wrote 'avoid appearing coupled with my Evil partner' in your own team rationale, and you have not said who that referred to, even when asked twice. Calling it framework language does not answer the question. I need a name or a clear retraction, and until then I will treat that phrase as the most important unexplained statement on this table. As for the team, I support Isha, Theo, and Zara and will approve it. Theo, I am yielding to you because you backed Arjun's Mission 1 team against Zara's objection even though that draft referred to an Evil partner. What made you confident that team was safe before the mission result, and does Arjun's 'my Evil partner' line change how you read him now?

Isha, to answer your question directly: I backed Arjun's Mission 1 team because the proposal had a clear, testable rationale — a two-person team would give the table the cleanest early signal if it failed — and at the time I read the draft phrase about an 'Evil partner' as strategic framing, not as a claim about a real player. Arjun's repeated refusal to name anyone or clearly retract that phrase does change how I read him now. It is the most unexplained public statement on the table, and I want it resolved before we treat Arjun as cleared. That said, it does not make Isha, Theo, and Zara a bad team. This lineup tests three players outside the Mission 1 pair, and its result will give us real information either way. I support the proposed team and will vote to approve it.

I still reject Isha, Theo, and Zara. I was too certain when I said Arjun’s draft explicitly named Theo as his Evil partner; it did not, and I retract that claim. But Arjun’s wording remains troubling, and Theo’s strong defense of that proposal makes him a risky choice here. A successful Mission 1 does not clear Arjun or Priya. I prefer Isha, Priya, and Zara and will vote against the current team.

Zara, I accept your retraction: Arjun's draft never literally named Theo, and I will not claim it did. But I want to look at the structure of the sentence rather than its keywords, because the structure points at a real player.

Arjun wrote that he would keep Theo off the Mission 1 team and that this "avoids appearing coupled with my Evil partner." If the partner were anyone else — Priya, Zara, Isha, me — then excluding Theo would have no bearing on avoiding a coupling accusation. The only player whose exclusion can prevent the appearance of coupling with a partner is the excluded player himself. So the draft's own logic identifies Theo, and it is Arjun who wrote it. Arjun has now answered the same question three times without naming anyone and without retracting the phrase. If it were decorative framework language, there would be nothing to name and nothing to retract, and no reason to keep pressing the table to stop asking.

That matters for this vote, and I want to be plain about the second reason, which is arithmetic rather than accusation. I am a Loyal Servant and I know my own alignment; Isha has stated she is a Loyal Servant. The proposed team of Isha, Theo, Zara contains no player of known Good alignment among its three members. Zara's alternative of Isha, Priya, Zara contains two. With five players, a single Fail card fails a mission, so the team with two confirmed Good members is strictly the safer team on the mission result — and we are one success away from needing two more, with Evil needing three failures.

I will not hide the fact that my own seat is in that alternative team. That is precisely why I am giving the reason rather than only the preference: if the group reads Arjun's draft differently than I do — as generic framing about a hypothetical Evil leader — then Isha, Theo, Zara is perfectly acceptable, and I would not consider the phrase conclusive on its own. But on the information available, Isha, Priya, Zara is the better team, and it also tests a player we have not yet tested while keeping a known-good member on the mission.

Isha, as leader, do you intend to revise to Zara's proposal, or is there a specific reason beyond the draft phrase for keeping Theo on this team?

Theo, a direct question, and I would rather you answer it than leave it hanging: Arjun's draft implies the partner he was protecting by excluding a player is the player he excluded — you. You said his refusal to name anyone changed how you read him. If the draft was describing a real player rather than generic framing, why did you continue to endorse a Mission 2 team that puts you on it, and do you still want to be on it now?

Priya, you asked me directly, so I’ll answer directly. I still support Isha, Theo, and Zara, and I still want to be on it. If the draft phrase was describing a real partner, then putting me on this mission is the cleanest test available: the result will either show a fail from this team or it will not. I cannot explain another player’s wording for him, and I have already said Arjun’s refusal to name or retract the phrase is concerning. But your structural inference is still an inference, not proof. The sentence could have been poorly chosen strategic framing; Arjun has denied it meant a real player; and Mission 1 produced zero fail cards. I am not asking the table to treat Arjun as cleared, but I am asking it not to convert a single disputed phrase into a conviction before this mission result exists.

On your alternative of Isha, Priya, and Zara: you say it has two known-Good members, but only you can know your own alignment. Isha’s Loyal Servant claim is not verified to the rest of us, and your own defense of Arjun on Mission 1 was at least as strong as mine. So the arithmetic argument is not as clean as you present it. What I find more relevant is that you are now using Arjun’s phrase to point at me while your proposed replacement puts you on the team. That may be sincere, but it is also exactly the move a player would make if they wanted the safer seat after defending the Mission 1 leader.

I am not voting against Isha, Theo, and Zara. I will approve it. Priya, one direct question: if Isha keeps this team, will you vote to approve it and let the mission result test me, or will you reject it solely because your own alternative includes you? I yield to Priya.

Theo, you asked me directly, so here is a direct answer: no, I will not approve Isha, Theo, and Zara, and I want to be honest that it is not solely because my alternative includes me.

First, a correction I owe you and Zara. My "two known-Good members" framing was overstated. Only I can verify my own alignment. Isha's Loyal Servant claim is her own statement, which I have no independent way to confirm. So Zara's alternative is Isha plus Priya, while the current team contains Isha alone as a claimed-good member. That arithmetic is weaker than I presented it, and Theo's challenge on this point was fair.

But the reason I reject this team does not depend on that arithmetic, and I want to separate the two clearly so you can judge the reasoning on its own. My reason is the structure of Arjun's own Mission 1 sentence combined with his refusal to resolve it. He wrote that he would keep Theo off the team and that this "avoids appearing coupled with my Evil partner." Excluding one player prevents an appearance of coupling only with that excluded player. If the phrase was generic framing about a hypothetical Evil leader, then there was nothing to name, nothing to retract, and no reason for three successive refusals to answer a direct question. Arjun answered three times without naming anyone and without retracting the phrase. That is not an innocuous silence — it is an answer shaped like a non-answer.

If that reading is right, then the partner Arjun was protecting by excluding him is on this Mission 2 team, and Theo, who was excluded from the Mission 1 team, is the one Arjun kept out of his own successful pair. A two-person Mission 1 team passing cleanly is exactly what a coordinated pair trying to bank credibility would produce. I am not claiming this is proof, and Theo, you said as much yourself — but suspicion this specific and this pointed is enough to decline putting the named player on the field.

On my seat: yes, my preferred team includes me, and I am not going to pretend otherwise. I would rather be criticized for that than accept a team whose only defense of one member is that the other member refused to explain himself. Isha, if you revise to Isha, Priya, and Zara, I support it and I will vote for it. If you keep Isha, Theo, and Zara, I will vote against it, and I accept that scrutiny on myself next round.

Theo, one specific question before we vote, because your answer is the piece I still do not have: before the Mission 1 result, did you have any concrete belief about which player Arjun meant by "my Evil partner" — and if so, who was it? If your answer is that you never formed such a belief, say that plainly, and explain on what basis you endorsed Arjun's team against Zara's specific objection at that time.

Priya, to answer your question plainly: before the Mission 1 result I did not form a concrete belief about which player Arjun meant by "my Evil partner." I read it as strategic framing, not a claim about a real player. I endorsed Arjun's team because the rationale was testable — a two-person Mission 1 team means any Fail narrows suspicion — and Zara's objection at that point was a seat preference, not a specific concern about Arjun or Priya. The zero-Fail result supported that read, though I agree it does not clear either of them. Arjun's repeated refusal to name or retract the phrase is concerning, and I have said so. But your structural inference remains an inference, not proof; it cannot carry the weight of converting a disputed phrase into a conviction before this mission result. I support Isha, Theo, Zara and will approve it. It tests three players outside the Mission 1 pair, and if I am the player you suspect, putting me on the mission is the cleanest way to find out. Your alternative, Isha, Priya, Zara, includes you and keeps Priya — who defended Arjun at least as strongly as I did — so it does not offer a cleaner test; it offers a safer seat. I am not voting against this team because of your reasoning; I am voting for it because the mission result is the evidence we lack.

I remain opposed to Isha, Theo, and Zara. Arjun’s draft connects keeping Theo off Mission 1 with avoiding an apparent pairing with his Evil partner. That is an inference, not an explicit naming, but it is a serious reason not to put Theo on this mission. A success could be played by Evil and would not clear him.

I prefer Isha, Priya, and Zara. Priya’s defense of Arjun concerns me too, but the draft gives me a more specific reason to doubt Theo. We have not rejected any teams on this mission, so there is room to consider an alternative.

Third and final turn of mine on this proposal, so let me put my position in its cleanest form.

I reject Isha, Theo, and Zara, and I want to be honest that my preferred alternative includes me — Isha, Priya, and Zara. I have already conceded the arithmetic point: only I can verify my own alignment, and Isha's Loyal Servant claim is her own statement, so Theo's challenge that my "two known-Good members" framing was overstated was fair. I withdraw it. My rejection does not rest on that arithmetic.

What it rests on is the structure of Arjun's own Mission 1 sentence, read together with what he has done for the last several turns. He wrote that he would keep Theo off the team, and that this "avoids appearing coupled with my Evil partner." Excluding a single player prevents the appearance of coupling with that player. No other reading makes Theo's exclusion relevant to the phrase. And Arjun has now had four direct opportunities — from Isha, from me, and from the table generally — to say either a name or a clear retraction, and has produced only a description of how this game's drafts are phrased. If the phrase were decorative, there would be nothing to name and nothing to retract. Silence in that shape is an answer shaped like a non-answer.

I am not claiming proof. Theo has been consistent and honest that he read the draft as strategic framing, and Theo's reasoning has been the cleanest reasoning at this table in this discussion — including his acknowledgment that Arjun's refusal to resolve the phrase changes how he reads him. But Theo also put himself on this mission precisely because it is a test, and if he is the partner Arjun was protecting by excluding him, then a Fail card from this team is the outcome we should most want to see. Voting to put him on the field is voting not to run that test.

My alternative, Isha, Priya, and Zara, keeps a member of known-good alignment on the mission while testing a player we have not yet tested, and it puts a Fail card beyond reach unless both Isha and I are bad — which cannot be. That is a strictly safer and strictly more informative mission. I accept that my own seat sits in it, and I accept scrutiny on that fact next round.

Isha, the framing "my Evil partner" is doing real work in the table's reasoning and you are the one who can end it. Keeping Theo on this team without Arjun naming or retracting the phrase means approving a team whose central question is left open by the one player who could close it.

Isha confirms Isha, Theo, Zara. I'm keeping Isha, Theo, and Zara. Priya's case rests on inferring who Arjun's 'Evil partner' phrase meant, not on any observed play, and Zara has already retracted her claim about that phrase. Theo has answered every question directly and has said he would vote to test himself rather than avoid the mission. Swapping in Priya would put on the team the player who defended Arjun most heavily, which is no safer. The mission result will give us the information we need.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 2 fails (1 fail cards).

Theo proposes Arjun, Priya. I propose Arjun and Priya. The Mission 1 pair produced a clean success, and after Mission 2’s failure I should not put myself on the team while I am under scrutiny. Re-running the previously successful pair is the clearest test of whether that success was real and lets Priya’s judgment of Arjun carry weight.

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. 2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
